May be taken without regard to food; high-fat meal raises bioavailability ~40%
Former Category B; use only if clearly needed. Antiretroviral Pregnancy Registry 1-800-258-4263
HIV-infected mothers should NOT breastfeed (HIV transmission risk); tenofovir is secreted in milk
Adjust dosing interval if CrCl <50 mL/min; risk of acute renal failure / Fanconi syndrome

summary: Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) is an oral prodrug nucleotide analogue reverse transcriptase inhibitor active against HIV-1 and hepatitis B virus. It is dosed 300 mg once daily and used in combination antiretroviral regimens for HIV-1 and as monotherapy-eligible treatment for chronic HBV. It carries a BOXED WARNING for severe acute exacerbation of hepatitis B after discontinuation in HBV-infected patients, and as an NRTI-class drug is associated with lactic acidosis / severe hepatomegaly with steatosis. Key toxicities are renal (acute renal failure, Fanconi syndrome - requiring CrCl-based dose-interval adjustment) and decreased bone mineral density.
indications: HIV-1 infection in combination with other antiretroviral agents (adults and pediatric patients 2 years and older)
Chronic hepatitis B in adults and pediatric patients 12 years and older

dosage.n: Taken orally without regard to food

dosage.d: 8 mg/kg once daily (max 300 mg); tablet by weight band: 17-<22 kg=150 mg, 22-<28 kg=200 mg, 28-<35 kg=250 mg, >=35 kg=300 mg
dosage.n: For children able to swallow intact tablets; monitor weight and adjust
Dosing-interval adjustment for baseline CrCl <50 mL/min
Monitor renal function and clinical response closely

dosage.d: 300 mg every 7 days or after ~12 hours of cumulative dialysis
dosage.n: Generally once weekly assuming ~3 sessions/week of ~4 h each

admin: Take orally once daily, with or without food
Do NOT use with other tenofovir-containing products (ATRIPLA, BIKTARVY, COMPLERA, DESCOVY, GENVOYA, ODEFSEY, STRIBILD, TRUVADA, VEMLIDY)
Do NOT administer with HEPSERA (adefovir dipivoxil) for chronic HBV
Use only as part of an appropriate combination antiretroviral regimen in HIV-1 infection
Do not discontinue without informing the prescriber - risk of HBV flare
moa: Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate is a water-soluble diester prodrug of tenofovir, an acyclic nucleoside phosphonate (nucleotide) analogue of adenosine 5'-monophosphate. After absorption it is converted to tenofovir and phosphorylated by cellular enzymes to the active metabolite tenofovir diphosphate, which inhibits HIV-1 reverse transcriptase and HBV reverse transcriptase by competing with the natural substrate deoxyadenosine 5'-triphosphate and, after incorporation into DNA, by causing chain termination.

absolute: FDA label lists no absolute contraindications (None)
relative: HBV-infected patients - severe acute exacerbation of hepatitis on discontinuation (BOXED WARNING)
Renal impairment / CrCl <50 mL/min (dose-interval adjustment required)
Concurrent or recent nephrotoxic agents (e.g., high-dose or multiple NSAIDs, aminoglycosides)
History of pathologic fracture or osteoporosis risk (bone mineral density loss)
Coadministration with other tenofovir-containing products or with HEPSERA
Elderly (greater frequency of decreased renal/hepatic/cardiac function)
monitor: Hepatic function with clinical and laboratory follow-up for several months after stopping anti-HBV therapy (BOXED WARNING)
Symptoms/labs of lactic acidosis or pronounced hepatotoxicity (steatosis) - discontinue if they develop (BOXED WARNING)
Estimated creatinine clearance, serum phosphorus, urine glucose, urine protein before and during therapy
Signs of Fanconi syndrome / proximal tubulopathy (bone pain, fractures, muscle weakness)
Bone mineral density in at-risk patients
Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome in HIV-infected patients

preg: Former Pregnancy Category B. There are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women; use during pregnancy only if clearly needed. Animal reproduction studies in rats and rabbits at doses up to 14 and 19 times the human dose (by body surface area) revealed no evidence of impaired fertility or fetal harm. An Antiretroviral Pregnancy Registry exists to monitor fetal outcomes (1-800-258-4263).
lact: Tenofovir is secreted into human milk. Because of the potential for HIV-1 transmission and for serious adverse reactions in nursing infants, HIV-1-infected mothers should be instructed NOT to breastfeed. The CDC recommends that HIV-1-infected mothers not breastfeed to avoid postnatal HIV transmission.
renal: Tenofovir is principally eliminated by the kidney. New onset or worsening renal impairment - including acute renal failure and Fanconi syndrome (renal tubular injury with severe hypophosphatemia) - has been reported. Assess estimated CrCl in all patients before initiating therapy; in patients at risk, also assess serum phosphorus, urine glucose, and urine protein before and periodically during therapy. No adjustment for mild impairment (CrCl 50-80 mL/min). Adjust the dosing interval for CrCl <50 mL/min: 300 mg every 48 h (CrCl 30-49), every 72-96 h (CrCl 10-29), and every 7 days or after ~12 h of dialysis for hemodialysis patients. Avoid concurrent or recent nephrotoxic agents.
hepatic: No specific hepatic dose adjustment is provided. BOXED WARNING: severe acute exacerbations of hepatitis have occurred in HBV-infected patients who discontinue anti-HBV therapy including TDF - monitor hepatic function closely for at least several months after stopping. Lactic acidosis and severe hepatomegaly with steatosis (including fatal cases) have been reported; discontinue if clinical or laboratory findings suggestive of lactic acidosis or pronounced hepatotoxicity develop.

major: Didanosine - tenofovir increases didanosine concentrations; reduce didanosine dose (250 mg if >60 kg, 200 mg if <60 kg) and monitor for toxicity (pancreatitis, neuropathy); discontinue didanosine if toxicity occurs
HEPSERA (adefovir dipivoxil) - do not coadminister for chronic HBV
Other tenofovir-containing products (ATRIPLA, BIKTARVY, COMPLERA, DESCOVY, GENVOYA, ODEFSEY, STRIBILD, TRUVADA, VEMLIDY) - do not coadminister
moderate: Atazanavir - tenofovir decreases atazanavir levels; give atazanavir 300 mg with ritonavir 100 mg
Ritonavir-boosted protease inhibitors (lopinavir/ritonavir, atazanavir/ritonavir, darunavir/ritonavir) - increase tenofovir; monitor for tenofovir toxicity
HCV agents sofosbuvir/velpatasvir (EPCLUSA), sofosbuvir/velpatasvir/voxilaprevir (VOSEVI), ledipasvir/sofosbuvir (HARVONI) - increase tenofovir; monitor for tenofovir toxicity
Drugs eliminated by active tubular secretion (acyclovir, cidofovir, ganciclovir, valacyclovir, valganciclovir, aminoglycosides) - may increase tenofovir and/or coadministered drug
minor: Drugs that decrease renal function may increase tenofovir concentrations
interactions.food: High-fat meal increases oral bioavailability (AUC ~+40%, Cmax ~+14%) and delays Tmax ~1 h; a light meal has no significant effect. May be taken without regard to food.
interactions.alcohol: No direct pharmacokinetic interaction; avoid alcohol excess given risk of hepatotoxicity and steatosis.
interactions.diagnostics: May cause hypophosphatemia, glucosuria, proteinuria, and rising serum creatinine reflecting renal tubular injury.

serious: Severe acute exacerbation of hepatitis B after discontinuation in HBV-infected patients (BOXED WARNING)
Lactic acidosis and severe hepatomegaly with steatosis, including fatal cases (NRTI class effect; BOXED WARNING context)
New onset or worsening renal impairment - acute renal failure and Fanconi syndrome with severe hypophosphatemia
Decreases in bone mineral density / pathologic fracture
Immune reconstitution syndrome in HIV-infected patients
rare: Proximal renal tubulopathy presenting as bone pain, limb pain, fractures, muscle pain/weakness
emergency: Severe acute exacerbation of hepatitis B on stopping therapy (BOXED WARNING) - jaundice, rising transaminases, hepatic decompensation
Lactic acidosis / severe hepatomegaly with steatosis (BOXED WARNING) - dyspnea, abdominal pain, nausea/vomiting, weakness; can be fatal

monitoring: BOXED WARNING: Hepatic function (clinical + laboratory) for at least several months in HBV-infected patients who discontinue anti-HBV therapy - resumption may be warranted
Watch for clinical/laboratory signs of lactic acidosis or pronounced hepatotoxicity (steatosis) - discontinue if they develop
Estimated creatinine clearance before initiating and as clinically appropriate during therapy
In patients at risk for renal dysfunction: serum phosphorus, urine glucose, and urine protein before and periodically during therapy
Bone mineral density in patients with history of pathologic fracture or osteoporosis risk
HIV antibody testing should be offered to all HBV-infected patients before initiating therapy
CD4 count and HIV-1 RNA (HIV) or HBV DNA and ALT (HBV) for efficacy
counsel: TDF is not a cure for HIV-1; remain under a physician's care and continue combination therapy
Do not stop TDF without first informing your physician - severe hepatitis flares can occur in HBV-infected patients who stop
Take on a regular schedule and avoid missing doses
Report symptoms of lactic acidosis or liver problems (weakness, muscle pain, trouble breathing, stomach pain, nausea, jaundice)
Report reduced urination, ankle/leg swelling, or bone pain (possible kidney injury)
Avoid high-dose or multiple NSAIDs and other nephrotoxic drugs unless directed
Do not breastfeed if you have HIV-1
Avoid spreading HIV/HBV: do not share needles or personal items; practice safer sex with condoms
pk: Antiviral activity after conversion to active tenofovir diphosphate; oral bioavailability ~25% fasted
Serum Cmax at ~1 hour (fasted); food delays Tmax by ~1 hour
Supports once-daily dosing; eliminated by glomerular filtration and active tubular secretion
Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F); keep bottle tightly closed; do not use if seal is broken
pearls: BOXED WARNING: Severe acute exacerbations of hepatitis B have occurred in HBV-infected patients who discontinue anti-HBV therapy including TDF - monitor hepatic function clinically and with labs for at least several months after stopping; resume anti-HBV therapy if appropriate. Lactic acidosis and severe hepatomegaly with steatosis (an NRTI class effect, including fatal cases) can occur - discontinue if lactic acidosis or pronounced hepatotoxicity develops.
TDF is a prodrug of tenofovir; oral bioavailability is ~25% and is increased by high-fat meals
Renal toxicity is dose/exposure related - adjust dosing interval by CrCl and avoid nephrotoxins; watch for Fanconi syndrome (hypophosphatemia, glucosuria, proteinuria)
Decreased bone mineral density is a recognized effect - assess BMD in at-risk patients
Offer HIV testing to all HBV patients before starting; HBV/HIV coinfected patients need a full antiretroviral regimen
Tenofovir is efficiently removed by hemodialysis (extraction ~54%)
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as remembered, then continue the regular once-daily schedule. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose - do not double up. Do not discontinue without consulting the prescriber because of the risk of hepatitis B flare.
overdose: Limited clinical experience exists above the 300 mg therapeutic dose (600 mg for 28 days produced no severe reactions). Monitor for evidence of toxicity and provide standard supportive care. Tenofovir is efficiently removed by hemodialysis (extraction coefficient ~54%; a 4-hour session removes ~10% of a 300 mg dose).
